content: 1. Bishop et al. (2013) conducted a study examining the specialized housing and transportation needs of adults living with multiple sclerosis. The research highlighted the unique challenges faced by this population in accessing appropriate housing and transportation services. 2. Rosenberg et al. (2012) investigated perceived environmental restrictions on the participation of children with mild developmental disabilities. The study focused on barriers within home, community, and educational settings that limit these children's ability to engage in daily activities. 3. Roy et al. (2008) explored the experiences of parents adapting their homes for children with motor disabilities. This qualitative study provided insights into the challenges and emotional impact of the home adaptation process. 4. Shyu et al. (2004) examined environmental barriers and mobility issues in Taiwan, applying the Roy Adaptation Model to assess its relevance in addressing these challenges. 5. Steultjens and Clemson (2006) reviewed a preventative home safety program for older adults with low vision. The program was found to reduce falls and was more cost-effective than exercise-based interventions. 6. Stineman et al. (2011) studied the relationship between activities of daily living (ADL), chronic health conditions, and the lack of home accessibility features among elderly individuals living in the community. The findings emphasized the importance of accessible home environments in supporting independence. 7. Stineman et al. (2012) further explored the impact of physical and social home environments on nursing home use among older adults. The study highlighted the role of home accessibility in delaying institutionalization. 8. Szanton et al. (2011) piloted the CAPABLE program, which aimed to improve function and health-related quality of life in low-income older adults with ADL difficulties. The program included home modifications and handyman services, though accessibility improvements were not directly linked to the intervention's success. 9. Torrington (2009) discussed the design of technology and environments to support enjoyable activities for individuals with dementia. The study emphasized the role of assistive devices in enhancing quality of life. 10. Van Hoof and Kort (2009) proposed a conceptual framework for designing supportive living environments for older adults with dementia. The paper outlined key considerations for creating dementia-friendly dwellings. 11. Wahl et al. (2009) reviewed empirical evidence on the relationship between home environments, modifications, and disability-related outcomes in aging individuals. The findings underscored the importance of tailored home adaptations. 12. Werngren-Elgström et al. (2008) conducted a 10-year longitudinal study on the relationship between person-environment fit, ADL dependence, and subjective well-being among older Swedish adults. The study revealed that changes in environmental fit significantly influenced ADL performance and well-being. 13. York (2009) examined residential design and outdoor area accessibility, discussing the implications of related legislation on improving access for individuals with disabilities. 14. Young (2012) provided an informative overview of effective home modifications for individuals with low vision, emphasizing practical strategies to enhance safety and independence. 15. Ahmad et al. (2013) evaluated the effectiveness of home modifications on the quality of life of wheelchair-using paraplegic individuals. The study demonstrated significant improvements in life satisfaction following interventions such as wheelchair-accessible doors, ramps, and non-slip surfaces. 16. Brunnström et al. (2004) assessed the impact of lighting adaptations on the quality of life of individuals with low vision. The study found that improved lighting significantly enhanced participants' ability to perform daily activities. 17. Campbell et al. (2005) conducted a randomized controlled trial to prevent falls in individuals aged 75 and older with severe visual impairment. The study found that home safety interventions were effective in reducing falls but not fall-related injuries. 18. Carlsson et al. (2017) investigated the effects of housing adaptations on falls and fear of falling among Swedish adults. The study found a significant reduction in fear of falling at three months post-intervention, though this effect was not sustained at six months. 19. Edgren et al. (2015) evaluated a home-based physical rehabilitation program for older adults recovering from hip fractures. The program demonstrated positive effects on physical disability without any intervention-related adverse events. 20. Fänge and Iwarsson (2005) conducted a longitudinal study on changes in ADL dependence and usability following housing adaptations. The study highlighted the long-term benefits of targeted home modifications. 21. Gitlin et al. (2006, 2009) examined the long-term effects of home interventions on mortality and functional difficulties in older adults. The findings suggested that in-home occupational and physical therapy interventions significantly reduced mortality rates. 22. Heywood (2004) reviewed the health outcomes of housing adaptations, emphasizing their role in improving safety and independence for individuals with disabilities. 23. Maggi et al. (2018) explored the determinants of falls and the role of occupational therapists in implementing home modifications to prevent falls. The study highlighted the importance of tailored interventions. 24. Norin et al. (2017) investigated the relationship between housing accessibility and participation among older adults with long-standing spinal cord injuries. The study found that accessibility issues were significantly associated with reduced autonomy and participation. 25. Petersson et al. (2008, 2009) conducted longitudinal studies on the impact of home modifications on everyday life for individuals aging with disabilities. The findings demonstrated improvements in usability and ADL performance following adaptations. 26. Slaug et al. (2017) analyzed the short-term costs and long-term benefits of improved housing accessibility for older adults in Sweden and Germany. The study highlighted the economic and functional advantages of accessibility interventions. 27. Stark (2004) demonstrated that removing environmental barriers in the homes of older adults with disabilities significantly improved occupational performance. 28. Tchalla et al. (2012) evaluated the efficacy of simple home-based technologies combined with monitoring systems in reducing falls among frail older adults. The study found significant reductions in fall rates. 29. Tongsiri et al. (2017) assessed the impact of home modifications on individuals with physical disabilities in Thailand. The study found improvements in functional abilities, except for those with severe difficulties. These studies collectively emphasize the critical role of home modifications, environmental design, and tailored interventions in improving the quality of life, safety, and independence of individuals with disabilities or functional limitations.
